title: Swiss glaciers lost 5.5% of their ice in one year, the second-worst year on record
body: On 1 October 2026, Glacier Monitoring Switzerland and the Swiss Academy of Sciences reported that Swiss glaciers had lost 5.5% of their ice in the year to 30 September, second only to 2022, and almost 20% since 2021 ([report](https://www.unifr.ch/webnews/content/20/file/annualrep_2026.pdf)). A glacier keeps a yearly budget: snow is added in winter, and snow and ice melt in summer. High up, some snow normally outlasts the summer and turns into new ice; lower down, more melts than falls, and the line between the two is where the year breaks even. In 2026 the glaciers began the summer with about 25% less snow than normal, June to August were the hottest on record, and the freezing level rose above 4,000 m on a record 76 days, so by September no winter snow was left even at the highest measuring stakes. Bare ice reflects only about half the sunlight, against about 90% for fresh snow ([NASA](https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/winter-in-southern-greenland-80082)), so once the snow is gone the melt speeds up.

slides.question: Between May and September 2026, on how many days was the freezing level above 4,000 m over the Swiss Alps?
slides.explanation: On 76 days, more than twice the average and a record, according to Glacier Monitoring Switzerland. Above the freezing level, snow and ice can melt.

slides.alt: Animation of an Alpine slope with a glacier under snow: 5.5% of Swiss ice lost in 2026. Winter adds snow, summer melts it, a break-even line divides gain from loss. Then a thin winter, record heat, the freezing level above 4,000 m, all snow gone by 2 July. Sunlight bounces off snow, sinks into ice.

slides.prompt: This toy glacier starts with a thin winter and a hot summer. How much snow, or how cool a summer, brings its yearly balance back to zero?
slides.takeaway: With normal snow, this toy glacier breaks even only if the summer freezing level stays near 3,100 m. Once its snow is gone, darker bare ice melts faster, so losses climb quickly.

steps.label: Winter snow piles up, most of all up high
Summer melts the snow, then bare ice
Above the break-even line, snow survives
Surviving snow is pressed into new ice

slides.heading: The two worst years for Swiss glaciers

left.label: 2022: record loss
left.text: On average 3.13 m of water lost over each glacier's area. Snow 32% below normal on 30 April, and Saharan dust darkened it.

right.label: 2026: second worst
right.text: On average 2.86 m of water lost: 5.5% of all the ice. Snow 25% below normal, the hottest June to August on record, less dust.

slides.label: the date in 2026 by which Swiss glaciers had melted all their winter snow, on average
slides.text: Glacier Monitoring Switzerland calls it the glacier loss day. It usually comes in August; in records since 2000, only 2022's came earlier.

slides.question: Why does a glacier melt faster once its snow cover is gone?
slides.explanation: Fresh snow reflects about 90% of sunlight and bare ice only about half, the US space agency NASA says, so bare ice absorbs about five times as much.

source.label: University of Fribourg: Swiss glaciers lose a further five per cent of their volume (1 October 2026)
